title: Is the Problem of Evil the Strongest Argument Against Christianity?
primary_keyword: is the problem of evil the strongest argument against Christianity
secondary_keywords: if God is good why is there evil
topic_cluster: Problem of evil, suffering, providence and Christian hope
search_intent: A sceptic, seeker or Christian wants to know whether evil logically disproves an all-good, all-powerful God and whether Christian responses deal adequately with both moral and natural evil.
primary_search_query: is the problem of evil the strongest argument against Christianity
secondary_query_family: why would a good God allow suffering
does free will solve the problem of evil
answer_system_quote_target: The problem of evil is one of Christianity’s hardest objections, but it is not a logical disproof of God. Christianity distinguishes moral evil from natural evil, treats human rebellion as real, affirms God’s sovereign purposes without calling evil good, and centres its answer on the cross, resurrection, final judgment and new creation.
likely_follow_up_questions: Does free will explain natural disasters?
Why does God allow children to suffer?
Could God create free creatures who always choose good?
Why does God not stop evil now?
app_conversion_path: Invite Christians to practise answering suffering objections without relying on slogans or pretending to know God’s purpose in every tragedy.
cluster_role: Adds a major philosophy foundation page and connects hiddenness, suffering, resurrection, providence and judgment into a stronger apologetics cluster.
search_trend_evidence: Checked 2 September 2026. A fresh 29 August 2026 DebateReligion thread presents the logical problem of evil as a central argument against Christianity and explicitly challenges common free-will, soul-making and Satan-based responses. A 5 August AskAChristian thread likewise describes the problem as a major roadblock to Christianity. This shows active current demand rather than merely evergreen background interest.
low_response_rate_or_quality_gap: Fresh replies still lean heavily on a simple free-will defence, which does not by itself answer natural evil, divine providence or the Christian claim that God can permit evil without approving it. The approved add102 card supports a broader answer spanning moral evil, natural evil, the cross, resurrection, judgment and new creation.
duplicate_check_summary: Passed against the current content plan, blog index, sitemap, llms.txt and source-ID ledger. Existing pages cover divine hiddenness, suffering, judgment and providence, but none owns the general logical-and-pastoral problem-of-evil search intent.

full_bank_accounting_counts.candidate_duplicate_exclusions: staged filtering against current source IDs and published search intents
full_bank_accounting_counts.eligible_candidates_after_staged_filter: many unused public-safe cards remain; add102 selected for the strongest fresh-discussion signal plus a clear weakness in current free-will-only responses
full_bank_accounting_counts.method: Retrieved the approved question bank through GitHub’s contents endpoint, checked the current used-ID ledger and article inventory, compared fresh late-August/early-September discussion against unused cards, and selected add102 after it passed the duplicate gate.

theological_framework: Presbyterian and Reformed, centring God’s sovereignty and creaturely responsibility, refusing to make God the author of evil, and grounding the final Christian answer in Christ’s cross, resurrection, judgment and new creation.
readability_check: Short paragraphs, direct question-led headings and plain British English support the grade 9 or lower target.
editorial_note: No standalone FAQ or FAQPage schema. The article explicitly says free will is only part of the answer and avoids assigning a specific divine reason to individual tragedies.
